topics.topic: Criteria for JSON number spellings to satisfy strict integer fields
questions: Are `1.0`, `1e0` and `-0.0` integral values, fractional values, or invalid inputs, and may they satisfy a strict integer field after canonicalisation?

Which JSON number spellings count as integers for a strict integer field: only integer-token spellings such as `1` and `-0`, or also mathematically integral spellings such as `1.0`, `1e0`, and `1.801439850948199e+16` that canonicalise without a fractional part?
Is integrality determined by JSON spelling, by the mathematical value, or by the parsed IEEE-754 value, and are forms such as 1.0 and 1e0 treated as integers?
Must an integer field accept mathematically integral spellings such as 1.0 and 1e0 after they canonicalise to 1, or only inputs originally parsed as an integer type?

quotes: canonical_bytes: [BEHAVIOR] MUST parse json_text as one JSON value and emit its RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical form encoded as UTF-8: object members sorted by the UTF-16 code units of their names, numbers written in the ECMAScript shortest round-trip form (an integral double without a fraction or exponent, so a number written 1.0 becomes 1), strings escaped exactly as JCS prescribes, and no whitespace; it applies no Unicode normalization, so two texts that differ only in normalization give different bytes.

answer_request: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST check one request in exactly this order, the first failure deciding: the byte length of request_bytes is within the imported RELEASE_CEILING_SURFACE_REQUEST_BYTES_MAX constant, else invalid_request; authenticate_token with presented_token gives an Actor, else unauthorized with one fixed reason that reveals nothing about any record; the depth check of the request message below, else invalid_request; for tools/call, the message names a catalogue operation, fits that operation's request model with no unknown field — a field typed X | None fitting when it is absent or JSON null; the fit is pydantic's in JSON mode, the request model's model_validate_json over the canonical JSON text of the arguments with strict=True, since strict validation of Python objects refuses an enum given as its value string and a tuple given as a JSON array, which is how every request carries them; a ValueError the fit raises (pydantic's ValidationError is one) is raised again as InvalidRequestError, so translate_failure answers invalid_request, never internal_error —, holds every bound below, measured on the fitted request before any JSON text in it is replaced, and has every JSON text it carries then made canonical by the replacement below, else invalid_request; the actor may call that operation by the actor table, else raise NotPermittedError; only then is the operation's handler called (A16 rule 1). initialize, ping and tools/list name no catalogue operation and are answered after the depth check, as the note on methods says.
judgement.why: State 8 validates strict integer fields from the canonical JSON form of the arguments, whose integrality follows the parsed IEEE-double value and ECMAScript shortest-round-trip spelling rather than the submitted token spelling.

topics.topic: Ordering and input values of canonicalisation versus strict request validation
questions: Which data is canonicalised, and does canonicalisation occur before or after strict request-model validation?
Does strict operation-schema validation run on the original parsed request values, or are arguments canonicalised and reparsed before that validation?

At what point are request arguments canonicalised relative to A16 rule 1's depth and operation-schema validation, and does the strict request model validate the original parsed arguments or values reparsed from canonical JSON?

quotes: answer_request: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST check one request in exactly this order, the first failure deciding: the byte length of request_bytes is within the imported RELEASE_CEILING_SURFACE_REQUEST_BYTES_MAX constant, else invalid_request; authenticate_token with presented_token gives an Actor, else unauthorized with one fixed reason that reveals nothing about any record; the depth check of the request message below, else invalid_request; for tools/call, the message names a catalogue operation, fits that operation's request model with no unknown field — a field typed X | None fitting when it is absent or JSON null; the fit is pydantic's in JSON mode, the request model's model_validate_json over the canonical JSON text of the arguments with strict=True, since strict validation of Python objects refuses an enum given as its value string and a tuple given as a JSON array, which is how every request carries them; a ValueError the fit raises (pydantic's ValidationError is one) is raised again as InvalidRequestError, so translate_failure answers invalid_request, never internal_error —, holds every bound below, measured on the fitted request before any JSON text in it is replaced, and has every JSON text it carries then made canonical by the replacement below, else invalid_request; the actor may call that operation by the actor table, else raise NotPermittedError; only then is the operation's handler called (A16 rule 1). initialize, ping and tools/list name no catalogue operation and are answered after the depth check, as the note on methods says.

answer_request: [FIELD_ASSIGNMENT] After every request bound is checked on the texts as received, as the last step of the fit check, before the actor check and before any handler runs, MUST replace every JSON text the request carries — the json_text of each RequestJsonValue and RequestConstant, the value_schema of every Port and RequestConstant, the guard_value of every EdgeGuard — by its canonical form obtained from canonical_bytes; a NonCanonicalValueError there is invalid_request, so modules below receive only canonical JSON (A01 rule 1). A text whose canonical form outgrows a bound it met as received is not refused here: the module that judges the value measures its canonical bytes, as start_run refuses a run input whose canonical bytes exceed the stored value ceiling.
judgement.why: State 8 fixes both stages: the whole arguments object is canonicalised and reparsed for strict request-model validation, while embedded JSON-text fields are replaced with their canonical forms afterward, following bounds and before authorization or handlers.

topics.topic: Value semantics for large integers changed or conflated by IEEE-754/JCS canonicalisation
questions: When distinct integer spellings map to the same IEEE double and canonical bytes, does the kernel treat them as one numeric value, retain their original arbitrary-precision integer values despite equal identities, or refuse one of them?

When an accepted exact integer's JCS shortest decimal spelling differs from its submitted digits, does the kernel retain the submitted mathematical integer for model validation and operation behavior, use the IEEE-754 value, or reparse the canonical spelling as a new arbitrary-precision integer?

When an accepted integer's JCS spelling denotes a different exact decimal integer but the same IEEE-754 value, does the operation and stored value retain the originally submitted integer or use the integer obtained by parsing the canonical bytes?

quotes: canonical_bytes: [BEHAVIOR] MUST parse json_text as one JSON value and emit its RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical form encoded as UTF-8: object members sorted by the UTF-16 code units of their names, numbers written in the ECMAScript shortest round-trip form (an integral double without a fraction or exponent, so a number written 1.0 becomes 1), strings escaped exactly as JCS prescribes, and no whitespace; it applies no Unicode normalization, so two texts that differ only in normalization give different bytes.
canonical_bytes: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns the canonical UTF-8 bytes only; the length of these bytes is the size of the JSON value wherever the kernel measures a value.

fit_port_value: [SCHEMA_CONSTRAINT] The schema check of a value port parses the port's value_schema and the candidate's canonical_json; for cardinality many the candidate MUST be a JSON array and every element MUST fit the schema, for cardinality one the whole value MUST fit it. Supported schema keywords are only — each optional, type included, an absent keyword constraining nothing — type (one of null, boolean, integer, number, string, array, object, given as one string), enum (non-empty array of distinct scalars), const (one scalar), properties and required for objects, additionalProperties given as true or false only, items (one schema) for arrays, minItems, maxItems, minLength, maxLength, minimum and maximum; integer means a number without a fraction; a schema that is not a JSON object or uses any other keyword ($ref, pattern, format, oneOf, anyOf, allOf and not among them) fits no value, so the schema check fails.

handle_start_run: [ORCHESTRATION] MUST turn each RequestJsonValue into a JsonPayload of the same port with its canonical JSON bytes, call start_run with the flow_id, those inputs and the actor, and show the RunAnswer it returns as a ShownRun.

runner_source: [BEHAVIOR] The program MUST load the code file as a module and call its top-level run once with a dict holding one entry per input port, read from the files its configuration names: a value port has exactly one file, its JSON decoded to Python — for cardinality many that file holds the JSON array, which decodes to the list itself and is never wrapped in another —; a file port of cardinality one its one file's bytes; a file port of cardinality many a list of its files' bytes in order; it writes a crashed message, with the type and message of the exception when one escaped, when the module fails to load, has no run, or run raises.
judgement.why: State 8 makes the JCS canonical bytes authoritative, so downstream validation, storage, operation behavior and sandbox decoding use the value obtained from those bytes rather than retaining the original arbitrary-precision spelling.

topics.topic: Acceptance of non-integral inputs whose fractions disappear under IEEE-754/JCS canonicalisation
questions: Must a non-integral input be refused when IEEE-754/JCS canonicalisation removes its fractional part, or is the resulting integral canonical value accepted?

What happens when IEEE-754/JCS rounding removes or changes a supplied significant fraction, such as a nonzero fraction that rounds to an integer or underflows to zero: is the value accepted and rounded, or refused?

quotes: canonical_bytes: [BEHAVIOR] MUST parse json_text as one JSON value and emit its RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical form encoded as UTF-8: object members sorted by the UTF-16 code units of their names, numbers written in the ECMAScript shortest round-trip form (an integral double without a fraction or exponent, so a number written 1.0 becomes 1), strings escaped exactly as JCS prescribes, and no whitespace; it applies no Unicode normalization, so two texts that differ only in normalization give different bytes.

canonical_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST first, before json_text is parsed, raise NonCanonicalValueError with a reason naming the depth when json_depth of the UTF-8 bytes of json_text — encoded with the surrogatepass error handler, so that a lone surrogate never makes the encoding fail and is refused below — exceeds the imported RELEASE_CEILING_JSON_DEPTH_MAX constant, so no parse recurses deeper than that constant; otherwise MUST raise NonCanonicalValueError, with a reason naming the first offending item in text order, when json_text is not one well-formed JSON value, when an object repeats a member name at any depth, when it holds a non-finite number (NaN, Infinity or -Infinity tokens, which the default Python parser would accept and therefore MUST be rejected explicitly), when a number written without a fraction or exponent lies outside plus or minus (2 to the power 53 minus 1) and fails both of two tests — the IEEE double nearest to it holds it exactly; it is written exactly as that double's ECMAScript shortest round-trip form —, or when a string holds a lone surrogate. Passing either test accepts such a number and only a spelling that passes neither is refused: 100000000000000000000, which a double holds exactly, passes the first, and 18014398509481990, the form JCS writes for 1.801439850948199e+16, passes the second although that double does not hold it exactly; so canonical bytes always parse again to the same bytes.

fit_port_value: [SCHEMA_CONSTRAINT] The schema check of a value port parses the port's value_schema and the candidate's canonical_json; for cardinality many the candidate MUST be a JSON array and every element MUST fit the schema, for cardinality one the whole value MUST fit it. Supported schema keywords are only — each optional, type included, an absent keyword constraining nothing — type (one of null, boolean, integer, number, string, array, object, given as one string), enum (non-empty array of distinct scalars), const (one scalar), properties and required for objects, additionalProperties given as true or false only, items (one schema) for arrays, minItems, maxItems, minLength, maxLength, minimum and maximum; integer means a number without a fraction; a schema that is not a JSON object or uses any other keyword ($ref, pattern, format, oneOf, anyOf, allOf and not among them) fits no value, so the schema check fails.
judgement.why: State 8 applies IEEE-double JCS conversion and exhaustively states its numeric refusal conditions, so a finite fractional spelling whose fraction is lost through rounding or underflow is accepted as the resulting canonical value and can then satisfy an integer schema when that canonical number has no fraction.
